articles.title: How one router caused the worst ground stop since 9/11
articles.summary: The mundane management failures inside the Trump administration and the FAA that led to the worst ground stop since 9/11.
articles.body: Today I’m talking with Darryl Campbell, a freelance journalist, aviation expert, and author of the book Fatal Abstraction: Why the Managerial Class Loses Control of Software. Darryl covers aviation and the FAA, and earlier this month, when the US suffered a sudden nationwide ground stop on air travel, Darryl was all over the story. He published a great report for us on The Verge about what happened, what and who was to blame, and what we might do about the underlying infrastructure failures in the aviation business. So ahead of Thanksgiving, one of the country’s major holiday travel weeks, I wanted to have Darryl on the show to walk us through this incident on Friday, November 13th, when the FAA grounded every departing flight in the country for more than four hours. You’ll hear us work backward from how a single router could cause this kind of damage to why our aviation infrastructure is so painfully out of date and what the government plans to do about it. Also, why incidents like this are creating a kind of swirling paranoia about AI and cyberattacks, even when the real culprit is far more mundane. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: aviation journalist Darryl Campbell on the FAA ground stop. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Darryl Campbell, you’re a journalist, you’re an aviation expert, and you’re the author of the book Fatal Abstraction: Why the Managerial Class Loses Control of Software, which is potentially the most Decoder title in all of publishing history. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks very much. Longtime listener, first-time caller. So thanks for having me. I love that book title. I love all the ideas that it suggests. We’ll have you back to talk about the book, but I feel like we’re going to use that idea to talk about air traffic control today on Decoder with you. Yeah, I think so much of what we’ve found out, even in the week since my report came out, has really just been a lot of boring management failures that have somehow cascaded to affect millions of people on thousands of flights. And it’s just the importance of actually having people who know what they’re doing in charge. There’s a lot there already. There’s a whole hour of Decoder right there. But what you’re referencing is the fact that you wrote a story for us about the nationwide ground stop the FAA had to call because of a bad router. Tell us what we know. What happened here? Why did air traffic control ground you all? --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- I’m going to take you back to Friday the 13th in a part of the country that nobody really associates with aviation, which is a little place called El Dorado, Arkansas. It’s the very tail end of part of this big backbone of data and telecommunications that’s really a private network run exclusively for air traffic control by a company called L3Harris, who runs it on behalf of the FAA. They’re just going in there, and they’re replacing what is essentially like 50-year-old infrastructure. If you remember back in the ‘90s, early 2000s when you made your first switch from DSL to fiber optic, that is exactly what they’re trying to do there, except- So just to remind everybody, DSL ran on the phone lines. Yeah, so this is like a cable modem. So I’m old enough to remember that, and maybe some of you out there are. But yeah, this is like as soon as you plug in fiber, your speeds get five to 10 times faster. And that sounds great, but in the private telecom world, that happens on entirely separate networks. Your DSL provider isn’t your fiber provider, or if they are, they’re running on parallel networks. The FAA system has to do both at the same time, and so you have to figure out how we get all of these different cables, different routers, different protocols for how these things transmit data to all play nice with the same reliability and uptime? Because you need that when you’re managing tens of thousands of flights every single day. One of the things that I think is really important to understand here is that the FAA runs its own private network. It’s called the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure. It was built by this contractor back in the ‘90s and early 2000s. So it’s old, and it is actually due to be replaced, correct? Yeah, and that’s part of the challenge, because you have to have it to keep the aviation system going; you can’t just shut it down for a week, rip everything out, and replace it. So they’ve been doing piecemeal upgrades over time, and a lot of it is done by this L3Harris contractor, who’s one of the biggest defense companies in the world. They’ve been working with the FAA for a long time. You would think that they would know how to do a simple router swap without causing everything to go down, but that’s exactly what happened on Friday. If you go back and look at everything that exactly caused the outage, it’s like a comedy of errors. No single thing would have caused the entire system to crash, but every little missed opportunity, failed connection, or decision that somebody made with no knowledge of what happens downstream from everything, really led to the point where all of a sudden the most congested airspace in the world could not figure out where the airplanes were. They couldn’t talk to people who are en route, and that’s a serious safety problem that could have put thousands of people at risk. Let’s work backwards from the actual precipitating incident, and then let’s talk about the government’s response to this crisis. So there’s a router swap that happens in Arkansas. In your story, you say they swapped in a fiber router for an old copper router, and that thing started sending out too many requests for the network it was connected to. Yeah. Explain exactly what that is. So L3Harris is trying to replace what is essentially a telephone switch from the 1960s with a new modern fiber optic data router. And so they’re removing the cabling, they’re removing the switch, and replacing it. Now, if you’re on, let’s say, a perfectly modern networking system, and you’re switching out a fiber optic for a fiber optic line, the data routing is the same; the protocols that the routers use to communicate with each other are the same. Do you remember that DSL to fiber optic comparison we made? That’s not really an issue because everything can handle huge amounts of data with high throughput. When the manufacturer sends out these new routers, there’s a factory setting on it that says, “Okay, when you’re making a communication attempt for the first time, assume that you are doing it with a high-throughput fiber optic system.” L3Harris forgot to turn off that switch, and so as soon as they plug in- That’s it? Yeah, from what I can tell and from all the reports that have come out, that is literally it. So L3Harris has said, “Hey, we did what we were supposed to. The router manufacturer said everything was working as it’s supposed to. There was no problem with the machine. It’s just that someone forgot to say, ‘Hey, you’re connecting to an old system.’” So when it starts pinging what it thinks is a high-capacity fiber optic data network, it’s just sending thousands and thousands of communication requests. Now, on their own, and if this wasn’t a critical infrastructural system, it probably would have done what I compare to a FaceTime call with bad Wi-Fi. All these connection requests start displacing some of the normal data packets that come through the network, and you start losing a couple of data packets, and so maybe the image quality degrades, or the audio starts to skip or something like that. That’s fine if you’re just trying to talk to someone in a normal one-on-one setting. But again, this is the air traffic control system for the world’s largest air traffic network, and you really can’t have any kind of data lag. And so what pilots start to see is the air traffic control routing centers that handle the high-altitude airplanes, the ones who are in cruise control and whatever; first, they start seeing some transmission loss. Sometimes it’s a radio transmission that cuts out. Over time, it gets worse as this router keeps pinging the system and keeps blasting it with all of these connection requests that cause data loss. And then that starts cascading. So it’s not just radio traffic. It then becomes radar data, too, and then it becomes so overwhelming that entire centers are going offline. At the peak of the crisis, when Secretary Sean Duffy decided to start this ground stop, 17 out of the 22 en route control centers around the country had gone dark, and they were unable to communicate with airplanes that were en route, or see where they were, without having to rely on a backup system. That strikes me as all very bad, and as we saw, there was a ground stop. Why did it take quite as long as it did for anyone to say what happened? Yeah. I’m thinking about [Transportation Secretary] Sean Duffy and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and their, frankly, absurd press conferences where they were saying conflicting things back to back from one another. They were not ruling out cyber attacks. What happened there? Why did it take so long to come up with what seems like a simple explanation for a very complicated problem? Yeah, well, if it sounded like people didn’t know what they were talking about, it’s because they didn’t. If you remember back in, I think, February of 2025, Elon Musk going in there with DOGE and firing a couple hundred people at the FAA. Now, you remember at the time — and in fact, I wrote a piece about it for The Verge — they said, “These aren’t safety-critical people. These aren’t the radar technicians. They’re not air traffic controllers.” That was true. But what they were was network engineers, data technicians, telecom specialists. These are the people who would have been overseeing the work that L3Harris was doing, and they simply did not exist. So there was a CNN report that came out about this trail of evidence, where usually what would happen is the contractor comes in with a router, and then an FAA technician meets them and oversees the work. They do some tests to make sure that everything is going okay and that nothing is going to disrupt the entire system. Everybody signs off, and then everyone goes home, and nobody really knows that anything happened. Well, guess what didn’t happen? The FAA technician did meet the contractor, but they didn’t oversee any of the work. The contractor didn’t say that they were done. They didn’t let the FAA know that they were going to start testing. All of these decisions and all of these theoretically simple, easy tasks related to basic good management and governance didn’t happen. By the time people figured out what was going on, we were already four hours into what was the worst ground stop since 9/11. How did we figure out what was going on? So eventually L3Harris started isolating parts of the data management system — basically taking routers offline. That’s why one of the initial reports came out and said, “Oh, we think we’ve isolated the problem to a part of the country that spans Arkansas and Texas.” And then, just one by one, taking these routers dark, they eventually turned off the single router that had gone and started creating these connection requests. Once that was offline, which honestly took them until around 7:40PM or 8PM ET on Friday, they were able, almost instantaneously, to start getting data and radar connections back. And then they decided to release the ground stop at that point. But it was really just your classic IT debugging of turning things off and seeing if anything changed until they found the right one. When all else fails. That’s right. Turn it off, turn it back on again. I said I wanted to move backwards. You stepped back to DOGE. Elon Musk comes in with DOGE. He takes the chainsaw to bureaucracy. He fires a bunch of network technicians. It seems like a bunch of processes go out the window. But this is a long story, right? This is a rickety system that we’ve known needed to be upgraded for years. Is it really just DOGE that brought us to the brink of incompetence, or is there a story beyond that? Yeah, I think it’s not just years, but decades. I mean, the main problem is that the money, effort, and sustained attention required to do all of these kinds of boring network upgrades operate on time horizons that are like five to 10 years. Whereas in politics, your time horizon is maybe a year or two max, every time you’re going back to budgeting, to getting the political will to get things passed. Because those things are so far out of sync, number one, it’s hard to just get the money in the first place to do these expensive upgrades. Number two, keep the money going so that the project is perfectly budgeted and the contractors have started on it, then get the money to keep doing the work that they need to do for a couple of years. And then number three, to maintain that momentum across administrations, across congressional changes, and really across party shifts. That’s been the big problem — that whenever a sort of smaller government, anti-regulation administration comes in, they start cutting some of the funding, and usually the FAA is on the chopping block. It’s almost kind of ironic that pilots, air traffic controllers, and the people who operate the system behind the scenes have actually gotten so good at making up for the FAA and the air traffic control system’s flaws — just because their machines are literally falling apart — that we’ve kind of papered over some of the issues and gone around some of the problems. If these had surfaced maybe five or 10 years ago, maybe we would be a little bit faster about getting the upgrades that we need today. Just continuing the theme of moving backwards, it’s not as though people didn’t know, right? There was funding to modernize the system. That funding was controversial in the way that whenever Democrats pass funding and Republicans take power, the funding becomes controversial. It’s funny. There’s a video of Sec. Duffy saying the Biden administration was wasting money that they should have been spending on the FAA. And then after this incident, he’s begging for $50 billion at a press conference. It seems like everyone knew about the problem, right? We have a plan to fix it. There’s a date to replace the system. Why isn’t there more urgency? Yeah, so I think there are two parts to your question here. I think number one is the political will required to get the budget in the first place, which is kind of like a two- to three-year process where you have to identify the company that can actually do the work. That’s part of the reason why we’ve got all these big incumbent defense companies because you can’t have some startup in San Francisco figure out how to change 3,000 miles of cabling overnight. That just can’t be done. And then you have to go through the work of getting it passed through Congress, through all of the accountability layers like the Government Accountability Office and all of the other procedural guardrails that are designed to keep government waste somewhat under control. That’s largely good, except that by the time we get the reports and actually figure out, okay, here’s what we need to do, here’s the right vendor, and so on, usually that’s after a midterm or after an administration change, and the political will has already kind of gone out the window. So I think that’s one part of it. And I think the second part is the FAA is just kind of suffering from death by a thousand cuts over the last 20, 30, 40 years. Even if they do the right thing, which is that they should be replacing a lot of these older switches with new routers, by the time that happens, all of the other issues with the administration and the agency have kind of filtered down to the point where they just don’t have the people in place. Let’s say you’re a network engineer who really knows their stuff and who could be in the right place for it. After three to five years of just sort of will they, won’t they, am I going to have a job next year, and all of the other things that get in the way of you being able to do your job, you’re probably going to go into private industry at that point. So I think there’s a talent problem and there’s this kind of overall political problem that’s really causing a lot of these issues. I want to rewind to the beginning of the second Trump administration, which feels like 10 million years ago, but it was not so long ago. It was two years ago. Elon comes in with DOGE; he’s got the chainsaw for bureaucracy, and he’s firing these people. He’s maybe getting rid of some of the talent you’re talking about. But there’s also a bunch of aviation catastrophes that happened, right? Planes were crashing, there were near misses at airports, and we heard a lot about how, because Elon was in the government, we would instantly modernize our infrastructure. We were going to rip Verizon out and replace it with Starlink. We were going to AI vibe code all the software. Did anything come of that, or did anything happen because of that? A couple of things have happened, but not to the extent that they’re addressing some of the major problems with the system. I think the biggest challenge here, and it’s kind of a quirk of the U.S. air traffic control system, is that our regulator and also the entity that operates all of the infrastructure and air traffic control systems are one and the same. It’s actually quite a hard thing for, in particular, Republicans and small government conservatives to get the idea that it’s good to fund the FAA when, in their mind, it’s a regulator as much as it is kind of the operator. That already creates a lot of challenges. I think the second thing that we talk about, and specific to DOGE, was that a lot of the contracts that they gave out were from people in that Silicon Valley orbit. So you think about Palantir; there’s a new company called ASI that’s now running the SMART AI air traffic control system. Oh, we’re going to go to ASI. Yeah, that’s been kind of a big conspiracy theory thing. But those are great, and they’re important systems, but the biggest challenges for the FAA are physical in nature. How do we replace this gigantic network? How do we get these telephone switches out of the ground and replace them with fiber optics? How do we replace radar and communications technology that is, in some cases, literally held together with duct tape and aluminum foil? And that part you’re never going to be able to do as kind of a small startup operating entirely in the digital and software space. I mean, the people that they gave contracts to and the people that benefited the most were attacking some small part of the problem, but not the one that’s related to how do you keep airplanes from not running into each other or how do you make sure that air traffic control radios are working so that helicopters don’t crash into commercial flights. Those are really hard, intractable, physical world problems that this sort of Silicon Valley AI vibe coding thing is never going to solve. There was some amount of drama about Verizon being ripped out and replaced with Starlink. The idea that we could just upgrade the networks and equip all the planes with new sensors — there was energy around that in the beginning of the Trump administration. It appears to have just completely fizzled. It’s part of this contractual incumbent thing. You can say whatever you want about replacing a vendor you don’t like with the one from your buddy down the hall, but it’s going to take years. Verizon, I think, did get moved out of some contracts, but they were replaced with another big telecom company, not Starlink. I mean, I’m pretty sure that there’s one Starlink system, and it’s operating in the middle of nowhere in Alaska. So on paper, yeah, Starlink has something, but again, they’re just not equipped to handle some of the big problems with all of this sort of legacy cabling and networking. You mentioned your buddy’s company down the hall. That brings us directly to ASI, which is the center of one of the hottest conspiracy theories about the ground stop that exists. Sean Duffy’s son, Michael Alfonso, is running for office. ASI contributed to his campaign. People have drawn this connection. They think there’s some sort of kickback, but ASI was hired to implement some AI-based system, or SMART system, that was going on while the ground stop happened. Are these things connected in any way? In a word, no. A lot of the conspiracy theories that have come up around this SMART system really came about in this gray space because the messaging from the administration was so bad, and there’s this natural antipathy towards AI. But all that SMART is doing is replacing some of the manual printouts and the routing that happens at the level of air traffic controllers in sort of control towers and facilities. They’re not actually plugged into the data backbone. They’re not handling any of the radar or the sensitive radio data. They’re just kind of a parallel system operating out in space. Now that being said, it’s because you’ve got the Secretary of Transportation and the Secretary of Homeland Security out there kind of shooting from the hip at their press conference that inspired exactly zero confidence in the messaging that they were giving. To give him a little bit of credit, Sean Duffy did say a couple of accurate things, but the way that he said them and then literally in the next sentence walked it back and said, “But it could be 10 other things,” does not inspire confidence at all. I think networking is a hard thing to explain to your average person because their eyes may glaze over, and then you have someone who really doesn’t understand it, who’s trying to do the right thing. But in his mind, the main point of that whole press conference was to get to that $30 or $50 billion shakedown of the government. So he’s kind of blowing past the technical details in the first place. It was just not a great look, and I think that’s why some of this conspiracy theory stuff has started to thrive. You mentioned the natural antipathy towards AI. Obviously, this ground stop happened in the context of many other outages. Microsoft Outlook went down. United had an issue that brought it down for several hours. There were other outages this week. There was a Chase Bank outage that people overread into thinking it was a banking system outage. There’s a lot of AI antipathy out there. There’s a lot of, “Well, this must be either AI-powered cyber attacks or everyone’s vibe coding garbage software and pushing into production; it’s crashing.” The top comment on your story is, “I call BS on this. It was AI, but we won’t hear it. They’re using this to beg for money they need after Elon Musk tore air traffic control apart.” Is there an AI element to this story at all? I would say to that commentary that it gets two out of the three, so that’s pretty good. The AI component, I think, is really more about what happens in three to five years when we fully transition, I’m sure, to this AI-powered system. I think that’s the part where we’re really going to see how good it is. Right now, air traffic controllers are still using legacy processes to route planes and keep track of everything. And those processes work pretty well. I mean, I’ve talked with hundreds of air traffic controllers over the years. They’re uniformly professional, very skilled, and more importantly, they know the ways that their systems will break down so that when something happens, they can immediately figure out how to keep things going without putting everybody at risk. When you do eventually move to the SMART AI system, that’s going to be a whole unknown. And I think that’s really kind of where my concern would be: when they turn it on for a larger portion of the air traffic control system, where they say, “Okay, from now on,” I’m just making this up, “Chicago is going to be on the SMART system, and we’ll see what happens.” That’s the day that maybe I would avoid flying for a little while. I don’t have the data to back this up, but it just feels like flying has gotten more chaotic and dangerous in the second Trump administration than before. There have been more crashes. Is that related to management incompetence? Is that just a string of bad luck? Chaotic for sure. I think dangerous, probably not. I mean, if you think about the incentives that line up, airlines do not want to have a crash. Passengers don’t want to fly on something dangerous. So with whatever’s going on at the administration level, there’s enough pushback within industry and within the passenger market that nobody is really going to take steps that they think will actively degrade the system. That being said, I would say you’re 100 percent justified in thinking that you should be less confident in the regulation and operations leadership side today than you would be five years ago. You heard it on Friday night and Saturday morning that the people in charge don’t really care what’s going on, and they just want the optics to look good. Even if you push them on the details, the people who knew what they were doing are really not in place anymore. I think we’ll probably see more of these disruptions over the next couple of years. I don’t think we’ll ever see anything that gets to the point of being materially more unsafe. In large part, I think the ground stop was probably justified. I mean, I talked to a bunch of controllers who said, “We could have handled it. We could have gone to backup systems, and in 20, 30, 40 minutes, things would’ve been more or less back to normal.” And I believe them. I think they absolutely could have handled some of these outages without causing any real safety risks. But from a passenger standpoint, you also don’t want to hear, and that’s part of the reason I started the story with that anecdote, “Hey, this is your pilot. We can’t communicate with anybody. We’re going to kind of see how it goes.” That is a very scary thing to hear. I think that really fuels a lot of it: that any kind of perceived safety risk in aviation just awakens this primordial fear in people. That’s totally justified. And I think it helps keep some of these anti-regulation impulses in check because people know that once a critical mass of people are afraid of flying, you kind of undo an industry that holds the entire United States and, in many respects, the world together. One of the things that’s really interesting about this dynamic, this whole story, is that if you were to design an air traffic control system from scratch today, it would be vastly more automated, right? Yes, absolutely. You would absolutely have an enormous amount of computer control over where the airplanes are. You would build vastly more powerful communication between planes and air traffic control centers in between them, and you would maybe even just let ATC control the planes directly, right? It’s a closed ecosystem where everyone wants to participate and has aligned incentives. You would just say, “Okay, the robots are going to fly all the planes for us, and they’re going to be perfectly safe.” But it doesn’t seem like there’s a pathway from here to there. At least not in the United States. I think there are so many counterarguments to some of the good intentions that people have, and frankly, a lot of people are just trying to get in because they want a hand of the government payout pie. I would be very worried if someone said, “Hey, tomorrow we’re going to launch robot planes coming out of Atlanta.” I do think a potential competing model is what we see in China, where they don’t have some of these competing economic or political gamesmanship kind of counterforces going on, where they are able to build what is essentially a new air traffic control system largely from scratch and with updated technology. And I think we are seeing some of the ways that automation is making that more efficient. That being said, I would bet you $100 that would never happen in the US, at least not until something materially changes in the way that the US thinks about air travel. I mean, we think about it as a right. We think about it as the primary way that we get from point A to point B other than driving a car for 100 miles, and we think about it as something that everybody should have access to. So, that means we want it cheap, we want it fast, and we’re kind of able to tolerate some of these large-scale disruptions as long as it doesn’t affect our Thanksgiving plans in a week. I think that also just kind of keeps the system the way it is in ways that maybe are not the case in some other countries that are newer to large-scale aviation. I like that you made reference to the cliché: you can have it cheap, fast, or good. Now pick two. Or maybe none. That’s what you’re saying. In this case, maybe none. There’s another argument I’ve heard, and this is in Project 2025. You mentioned the industry has a lot of incentives to figure this out, to make it good, to make sure people feel safe. In Project 2025, the idea that we should privatize air traffic control exists. At the beginning of the second Trump administration, as Elon was slashing air traffic control and the FAA, the notion that this would lead inexorably to privatized air traffic control that could then impose a bunch of this stuff, because the industry would be doing it to itself, was everywhere. I heard about it constantly. That doesn’t seem to have happened. Is there a push, is there an argument to be made for private air traffic control? We definitely saw that, and I think with Project 2025, that’s been a plank of The Heritage Foundation’s plan for government for more than two decades, if not since the late ‘80s when Reagan fired the air traffic controllers. I think privatization is a difficult concept for a lot of people to get their head around. But I do think the core idea, which is that you kind of need to separate the FAA as regulator from FAA as air traffic control operator, is fundamentally sound, whether that means moving it into a new government department or some other structural change. A lot of places around the world do have privatized air traffic control, so Canada, the UK, Germany, or they have a different system entirely. In Brazil, for example, air traffic control is actually controlled by the military. China is really the only big country that has a similar structure, but when you’re in a one-party system, it doesn’t really function as it does in the US. That is kind of a weird quirk that needs to be solved one way or another. The quirk is that the regulator also oversees air traffic control. Correct. But I just don’t know what the right pathway is because there’s also… I mean, you’re seeing it today with some of these contractors who are coming in and essentially scamming the government about everything, and that doesn’t seem to me like a safe way to operate the air traffic control system. How do you compensate for that human/corporate nature that we seem to have here, where you do kind of want to maximize profits even past the point of producing a good product? The airline industry is not full of shy characters. Ed Bastian, the CEO of Delta, is not a reserved figure. These are big personalities; they run big businesses, they battle with each other, and they spend enormous amounts of money. As you said, they’re the backbone of the global economy in many ways. Why can’t they push for it? Why aren’t they leading the charge? Ah, so there’s an interesting one. They are leading the charge publicly, while in private not really committing any considerable support to it. So let me put this in the context of aviation security. It costs the US government about $10 to screen for baggage, security, and whatever. But if you look at your airline ticket, your average FAA 9/11 fee, whatever it’s called today, is $1.50. That was because airlines pushed so hard against any kind of thing that would increase their fares that we’re essentially losing money on every security scan. Now, whether or not security works is a whole other story, but that’s kind of the mentality that they have. It’s great for them to pontificate about what we need, but if you ask the airlines to shoulder some of the burden, they’re going to say, “Well, this is going to blow up our entire economic model.” That’s a difficult thing to swallow. I mean, in Canada, they just make them pay for the fees. The security fee is about 10 times higher. The fees for their private air traffic control system also pass through to the passengers, but that means that they don’t have your $70 “go somewhere cheap this weekend” kind of fares that we do in the US. So there are trade-offs, and I think the industry isn’t yet willing to part with some of that margin in order to upgrade the air traffic control system. They think it should be a government burden to pay. If the listener is keeping track of us going backwards, we started with one router that was replaced with a misconfigured setting, and we’ve arrived at how we should split up the FAA and change the fee structure for airlines. That is a long and winding road, but it feels like a very direct connection. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, these kinds of changes take decades to do. If you’re in that short-term mentality, that one where you’re just trying to make it to the next election or you just need this particular line on the budget, you’re never going to get to a world where we can have a fully functional air traffic system. Part of the thing is that people do hide behind this complexity to both extract money from the government funds that are available or to just be able to… Case in point, Sec. Duffy, who, when he was a congressman, voted against funding for the FAA. Now six, seven, eight years later, he’s saying, “Oh my gosh, what a terrible idea. Whoever did that in the first place should be banned from the government. By the way, I also need $50 billion more to do it.” You can kind of see how short-term memory, the political cycle, and everything else line up to make sure that we kind of get the system we deserve in a way. Let’s say Sec. Duffy was massively competent. He was the single best network design engineer that has ever existed. This is a lot for a cast member of The Real World, but so it goes. What if you gave him $50 billion? If you dumped $50 billion on the FAA today, could it accomplish building a system that was reliable, stable, much more automated, and safer? I think it could happen in a couple of years, but it’s not just the money that you would need. I think you would need a couple of other things too. Number one, you just have to have the managers who can do it. So you remember Mark Zuckerberg; his whole thing was like, “Let’s get rid of all these middle managers.” But they have a function. And especially when you’re dealing with legacy systems, complex technical installations, and the management of just large networks of people, not just data, but people. You kind of need those people who are in these glue functions to make sure that, hey, maybe let’s not do something on a Friday afternoon when even a small failure is going to bring down a busy air traffic controller. Maybe let’s have a technician on site who knows what they’re doing and who can oversee the work. Maybe let’s have a plan that says, hey, let’s check the factory settings when you plug in this thing. It’s not just these giant top-line initiatives of a lot of money. It’s the baseline competence process and the ability to take things slowly when you need to. All of that is missing right now. If you think too hard about it, you can get really frustrated and despair about the future of air travel. The thing that gives me confidence is that we’ve done it so far, even in these conditions where we’re not having massive numbers of crashes, and that we are willing to pause the system when it makes sense to do so. But you can only go on for so long like that. I think this is really when we’re coming to a decision point, and at some point the equipment itself, regardless of what the politicians say, regardless of what the budget says, the equipment itself is going to tell us, “This is unsustainable. We can’t go on anymore.” I would rather we do the work to not get to that point if we can, because I don’t want to be the person on the airplane who hears the pilot say, “Oh, we’ve lost communication with the FAA and really have no idea what’s going on.” That’s a very scary and dangerous thing to hear. We’re publishing this the Monday before Thanksgiving, which is historically one of the busiest air travel weeks of the entire year. Should people feel that the system is reliable right now? I think we’ll get through Thanksgiving. [Laughs] That was a long pause, dude. Well, I was going to say that I’m staying put this Thanksgiving, so make what you will of that. I think the system, airlines, know what’s going on. Now people are on guard for that. And from what we’ve heard from the FAA, they’re not installing any new routers anytime soon. That particular risk is pretty much eliminated. I would say your safety has never really been at risk, and people are still able to manage these crises when they happen. So I wouldn’t worry about safety. I would say give yourself a couple of extra hours either way. For example, I flew to Boston over this past weekend. Saturday morning, even though the ground stop had been lifted, we were still delayed over an hour. It was not because of any communications problem, but because so many things had happened to put airplanes and people out of place that they were literally calling flight attendants on their day off to come in and work, and that’s what my aircraft was waiting for. Recovery will happen. Disruptions can be managed to a certain extent. But I think if we get to another year from now and we’re still paralyzed in this world of, “Well, let’s just spend the time pointing fingers rather than doing anything meaningful,” then I think it really starts to call into question whether we do have the capacity to fix what’s wrong with the air traffic system. FTI, the network at issue here, is due to be replaced in 2028. Just to wrap it up, what are the markers you’re looking for to see if that process is happening as intended and we are going to wind up with a better, more reliable network? I think by the middle of next year, we’ll be able to see the pace at which some of these projects are being implemented. And so we’ll know if there’s a problem with implementation that’s going to push out timelines for the next two to three years. I mean, the FAA has gotten really good at overpromising and underdelivering over the years. There was an entirely new air traffic control system that was supposed to be put into place between 2000 and today that just died because of a lack of political will. One of the good things that the FAA has done is actually created a website tracking a lot of these projects. And if you’re nerdy like me, you can go on there and see, okay, this week they put a router in there in Arkansas or wherever. And so that’s really going to tell us and give us the clarity that we’ve lacked over the last couple of years: the pace of some of these projects. And to give them credit, it is creating some accountability where there wasn’t really any. But I think it will really be monitoring over the next six to nine months to see whether this has fundamentally changed the FAA’s appetite for taking risks that will get to a better system down the road, but that may cause disruption today. And that’s really what I’d be worried about: that it’s easy and it’s practically agency policy at this point to kick the can down the road. And so if this has created so much blowback that the FAA is now completely risk-averse, there may be a world where they don’t accomplish some of these things until the 2030s. There is going to be a massively democratic Congress in power in just a few months here. All they can really do is oversight. I don’t think you want members of Congress doing the router upgrades. Yeah. They can do oversight. Do you think that oversight will lead to any meaningful change here? Or do we just have to wait until Sean Duffy and his band of merry managers are out? The one thing that I would like to see from the incoming Congress is a lot of the restoration of the jobs that were cut by DOGE back in 2025. These are the people who should be doing this, who should be overseeing it. I don’t care what the Secretary of Transportation or Congress is or isn’t doing, but you do need these managers in place. I think there’s a loss of those 400 people in the DOGE cuts, plus another thousand to 1500 retirements or just people quitting the FAA. You really want those people back because this is such a unique structure, and it’s such a unique kind of amalgam of partially obsolete, partially new technology. It’s the only thing like it in the world that I’m aware of. There’s only a certain number of people who even know enough to deal with it. You need those people in place before you can make those changes. So I think if Congress is willing to make changes to bring those people back, to restore those jobs, and protect the funding for those jobs from the next random idea that someone has, then I would say that’s a good change. If it’s just more theatrics and pushing budget lines from one section to another, that would give me less confidence. Darryl, this has been great. I feel like I could talk to you about this all day and all night. The book is called Fatal Abstraction: Why the Managerial Class Loses Control of Software. I feel like the ideas that we’ve talked about here are directly related to ideas in your book. Yeah, and there’s a whole chapter on org charts in there, just for Decoder listeners. Perfect Decoder bait. We’re going to definitely have to have you back very soon. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. All right. Thanks, Nilay. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! Decoder with Nilay Patel A podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems. SUBSCRIBE NOW!

articles.title: Dutch privacy authority urges consumers not to buy 'pervert glasses' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The Netherlands' data protection agency said smart wearables violate people's privacy, get information wrong, and can result in unsafe situations.
articles.body:
The Dutch Data Protection Authority is urging consumers not to buy AI-enabled camera glasses, warning that they compromise the privacy of nearby bystanders and risk the safety of their users.

The authority, whose recent statement falls just short of an outright ban, said that use of the internet-enabled and always-on glasses to record people in public is “almost always prohibited.”

Critics have dubbed these smart wearables as “pervert glasses” for their propensity to be used to video people without their permission, particularly to harass women. While some glasses have warning lights when users are recording, privacy advocates have argued that these alerts are not clear enough. Some people have even made phone apps capable of detecting nearby smart glasses wearers.

The Dutch data protection authority warned that the glasses also produce wrong results and unsafe results. In one test carried out by the Dutch authority, a pair of unnamed glasses “gave dating advice to an adult who indicated that they are interested in a minor.” The glasses also incorrectly read a medicine label and claimed to have called an ambulance when it had not.

The Dutch government’s advice follows a similar move by the Norwegian government , which in September said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices.

articles.body:
Senate Democrats are debating whether to change the filibuster rules when they take control of the upper chamber of Congress in January.

What to do with the filibuster has emerged as an issue in the leadership race between Sens. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), and it’s also a dividing line as some Democrats look at how they can get legislation to President Trump’s desk next year.

Join The Hill’s editors and Senate reporter Alexander Bolton for a conversation on the topic. Plus, hear from tech reporter Miranda Nazzaro on the stunning news that Jensen Huang is returning as CEO of Nvidia.

articles.title: Hegseth’s former chief of staff calls for his resignation
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s former chief of staff called for the Pentagon chief to resign, arguing he botched the handling of the Iran war and criticized his former boss for firing dozens of senior military leaders and blocking promotions of military officers. “Pete’s ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s former chief of staff called for the Pentagon chief to resign, arguing he botched the handling of the Iran war and criticized his former boss for firing dozens of senior military leaders and blocking promotions of military officers .

“Pete’s ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have lost any ability to be effective,” said Joe Kasper, who was Hegseth’s chief of staff until April last year, in an interview with Politico published on Monday. “For that reason and others it’s time for Pete to call it quits.”

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

President Trump has stood by the Defense secretary, who recently survived an impeachment effort in the House led by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). Trump praised him for doing a “great job” in getting rid of “woke” generals.

The failed impeachment came after the president asked allies and advisers about Hegseth, The Hill previously reported . Trump’s decision to elevate adviser Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff also likely bodes well for Hegseth, as the two have a “very good” and “close” relationship, according to multiple sources .

But Kasper, an Air Force veteran, said the Defense secretary’s standing on Capitol Hill is on a downturn.

“He’s not just burned bridges up on the [Capitol] Hill. He’s napalmed them. … He’s going to be suffocated, and it’s not like it’s going to be a slow suffocation,” he continued. “It’s going to be a quick asphyxiation.”

Kasper added that he wanted to “speak truth to power” after Hegseth and a group of his advisers were yelled at earlier this month by an Army sentinel for breaking decorum at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery. A day later, the Pentagon leader awarded Spc. Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the “execution of his duties.”

The former official, who was briefly a special government employee at the Pentagon following his chief of staff stint, oversaw the firing of three top Pentagon officials last year, who were accused of leaking sensitive information to the news media.

“If we think you are leaking to the press, that’s a very real problem. We take that very seriously at the Pentagon,” Hegseth said last year on Fox News. “Disgruntled former employees are peddling things to try to save their ass, and ultimately, that’s not going to work.”

Hegseth’s senior adviser Dan Caldwell, former deputy chief of staff Darin Selnick and Colin Carroll, former chief of staff to the deputy secretary of Defense, were under leak investigation and were fired from the Pentagon in April 2025. All three have denied accusations.

Caldwell was hired by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence earlier this year, and an administration official told The Hill at the time he had not committed any wrongdoing.

“There was no evidence released to suggest Mr. Caldwell had, in fact, leaked information from the Pentagon,” the official said. The matter was investigated, and he was cleared.”

articles.title: Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
articles.summary: Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends.
articles.body: Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you. Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled. [Media: [Media: And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. Shivon Zilis, who has two children with Musk, also got in on the fun. [Media: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, is a man who can relate to Huang’s struggle. [Media: Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own. [Media: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear. [Media: Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke took what one could call a moral stance. [Media: And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one, but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first. [Media: Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire also pointed out the obvious market-bending powers of Huang’s reinstatement. [Media: Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news? Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.” In the same appearance, Trump said “we need to protect our geniuses.” Marc Andreessen didn’t officially comment on the reinstatement, but the a16z cofounder changed his X bio after the news broke. It now reads: “We have to protect our geniuses.” Trump also seems to be relishing in Huang’s alleged affairs. In another Truth Social post, he superimposed Huang — red bra in hand — into the iconic photo of his reaction to being shot at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. [Media: For Canadian venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Trump’s intervention is just further proof of Huang’s innocence. Certainly an interesting take! [Media: The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per Odd Lots host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess. Update, November 23rd: This post has been updated with reactions from Shivon Zilis, Tobi Lütke, Shaun Maguire, Chamath Palihapitiya, and Marc Andreessen.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $44 billion | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The cybersecurity giant said that the deal to buy Zscaler, which provides zero-trust products to large enterprises, will better equip their customers to use AI agents.
articles.body:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday.

CrowdStrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.

Zscaler is a San Jose, California-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.

CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones, and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.

In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.

The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

articles.title: Trump says he ‘convinced’ Nvidia board to reinstate Jensen Huang

articles.body:
President Trump said Monday that he “convinced” the Nvidia board to reinstate embattled CEO Jensen Huang.

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC . “And I convinced them.”

Huang was reinstated Monday, just more than a week after he stepped down amid an affair scandal, including one with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump continued, referring to Jensen Huang’s reinstatement. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was to me a very important part of our country.”

The Nvidia board said it “believes Jensen in the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company,” Harvey Jones, the tech firm’s board chair, said in a statement.

The panel said it received input from “senior levels” of the U.S. government , which gave the company confidence that his reinstatement poses no national security risk. But the board also said it would be continuing its own investigation .

Huang said he is “honored” to take the position back.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” he said in a statement.

Trump has been a consistent defender of Huang amid the controversy.

He told CNBC that the U.S. did a “thorough investigation” and it showed Huang did “nothing wrong.”

“We have to protect our geniuses,” he said.

The president has previously said he doesn’t know whether Alice Huang was actually a spy.

Trump said he thinks Jensen Huang will “start off on an almost higher level” as he returns to Nvidia.

“He’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate,” he continued in the interview. “That was probably, that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells.”

In a Truth Social post , the president said the country “needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”

articles.title: US selected as Women’s World Cup host site in 2031
articles.summary: The United States will host Women’s World Cup matches in 2031, five years after the men’s tournament brought millions of international travelers to the country this summer and earned FIFA its most profitable Cup in history. Along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, the U.S. will host matches during the first women’s tournament to feature…
articles.body:
The United States will host Women’s World Cup matches in 2031, five years after the men’s tournament brought millions of international travelers to the country this summer and earned FIFA its most profitable Cup in history.

Along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, the U.S. will host matches during the first women’s tournament to feature 48 teams, FIFA announced Monday.

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will host matches in 2035, the federation said.

It will be the first time since 2003 the Women’s World Cup, launched in the early 1990s, will be played on U.S. soil.

“Our objective, of course, is making women’s football truly global, and to build the future together with all Member Associations and with all stakeholders,” FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in a statement. “Today, we decide here on the hosts of the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2031 and 2035. This is a proud moment for you, this is a proud moment for us, for all of us.”

Soccer, as it is known in the United States, has exploded in popularity in America since the Women’s World Cup was launched and the U.S. hosted the men’s tournament in 1994.

This summer’s edition of the cup generated billions of dollars in revenue for FIFA, with television ratings breaking records for global soccer and Spain taking home the title for the first time since 2010.

Infantino’s future atop FIFA, however, has been an open question heading into the federation’s coming election cycle next spring.

The federation’s chief executive has faced intensifying allegations related to corruption and self-dealing and his coziness with President Trump in the run-up to this year’s men’s tournament, and he has given rise to questions about the U.S. government’s relationship with FIFA during Trump’s second term.

The U.S. women’s team has had steady success in the World Cup, claiming four titles, most recently in 2019.

“Football belongs to everyone, everywhere in the world, and we have to create opportunities, we have to create development, we have to create infrastructures,” Infantino said as part of his Monday statement. “We need resources, as well, to be able to make this happen. And together, we will have a real impact.”

articles.title: Ukraine was behind attack on Russian warship off Libya: Zelensky
articles.summary: Ukrainian drones sank a Russian naval ship in a Libyan port ​on Sunday, according to President Volodymyr ‌Zelensky. In videos released by the Ukrainian leader on Monday, the corvette known as the Merkury — one of Russia’s newest vessels — is shown being attacked at the Benghazi naval base. Ukraine’s SBU security service captured the…
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones sank a Russian naval ship in a Libyan port ​on Sunday, according to President Volodymyr ‌Zelensky.

In videos released by the Ukrainian leader on Monday, the corvette known as the Merkury — one of Russia’s newest vessels — is shown being attacked at the Benghazi naval base. Ukraine’s SBU security service captured the event, during which seven maritime drones were launched from a mothership and smashed into the side of the ship, causing explosions and smoke to billow from the vessel.

Another drone attack off the coast of Libya struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which ‌Zelensky said had been used to transport weapons.

“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” ‌Zelensky said, noting that Russia had tried and failed to counter the strikes on the ​Merkury.

He added that Ukraine also destroyed a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter and that forces will “continue operations in designated waters.”

The attacks come a day after a drone struck a Russian military-linked cargo ship, the Sparta II, in the Baltic Sea in the Gulf of Finland. The 16-member crew was forced to evacuate and was rescued by a nearby Russian ship. The vessel drifted into Finland’s waters but is now being towed back ​to Russian territory, Reuters reported .

Finland’s military said Ukraine was likely responsible for the strike , which occurred in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island. Ukrainian officials have not publicly claimed responsibility.

“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote Saturday on the social platform X . “The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Moscow on ​Monday accused Ukraine ‌of engaging in “terrorist activity” in the ​Baltic Sea incident.

The attacks off Libya and Finland are a rare case of Ukraine apparently striking Russian ships outside the Black Sea and come as U.S.-backed talks between Kyiv and Moscow resumed this month. The two sides appear to have made little progress, however.

A Russian drone struck an apartment building north of Kyiv on Sunday, killing at least four and leaving up to a dozen more people buried in the rubble.

articles.title: Trump says courts, incoming Iowa gov should sign off on lead detonation
articles.summary: President Trump is potentially pausing a forthcoming detonation of lead-containing munitions in Iowa, saying the ultimate decision on whether to move forward will be up to both the courts and incoming Democratic Gov. Rob Sand. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he backed the detonation, but would not move it forward without permission…
articles.body:
President Trump is potentially pausing a forthcoming detonation of lead-containing munitions in Iowa, saying the ultimate decision on whether to move forward will be up to both the courts and incoming Democratic Gov. Rob Sand.

In a post on Truth Social , Trump said he backed the detonation, but would not move it forward without permission from both Sand and the courts — and he said they would be responsible for any adverse impacts of not moving forward.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump wrote.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” he added.

The Army was poised to detonate the munitions last week but had postponed the action to this Wednesday amid public outcry.

It has said in official documents that handling the munitions in a controlled way would be better than leaving them alone because it would avoid the risk of an “accidental, uncontrolled detonation” that could lead to “catastrophic damage.”

In a statement released later Monday , Sand called for greater transparency while declining to take a firm position on the detonation.

“The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks. Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” the governor-elect said.

“That means they should have the same access to the information I’ve received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source. I’ve asked the federal government to share that information with the public as soon as possible,” Sand added.

Separately, environmental organizations have challenged the Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency permit for the Army’s action in court.

In an email, Rachel Rintelmann, managing attorney at Earthjustice, said that Trump’s post “only adds further confusion to a situation that has already caused chaos in the lives of impacted communities.”

“If the Army has changed its plans, it has a duty to inform the public. The people of Iowa deserve better than this,” Rintelmann said, noting that the suit challenges the permit, not the actual detonation. She added that if there is a true emergency, the Army should act in the public’s interest.

articles.title: How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left and rejoined the AI chip giant in a span of just a few weeks. Here’s how we got here.
articles.body: The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago cofounded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.” Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman — Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. So when Huang resigned less than two weeks ago, the decision seemed final. Even Nvidia’s board appeared unwilling to budge. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” board chair Harvey Jones said during an earnings call last week. But in the days following Huang’s resignation, the founder’s allies — including President Donald Trump — mounted a pressure campaign that brought him back to the company he created and sent Nvidia’s share price rocketing upward, almost as though he had never left. The campaign in support of Huang began almost immediately after his resignation. A coterie of tech leaders began posting in support of Nvidia’s founder: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney questioned the motives of journalists who broke the stories about his affairs. Tesla CEO Elon Musk likened Huang’s departure to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman later said on stage, “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.” "“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”" - Donald Trump Meanwhile, some of those tech leaders began questioning aspects of the reporting that led to Huang’s exit. Venture capitalist and former White House AI czar David Sacks cast doubt that Alice Huang was a spy, citing a lack of confirmation from US officials. Trump exacerbated the uncertainty, telling reporters, “I don’t know that she is a spy,” despite reports saying the assessment had relied on US intelligence sources. Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, found itself in a tough position. The company’s shares crashed following Huang’s departure, and they didn’t pick up even after a rosy earnings report. The board was also scrambling to find a new CEO, something industry analysts speculated would prove exceptionally difficult. Reports indicated that Nvidia was considering hiring Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, both of whom already have powerful roles in the chip industry. Trump quickly warmed up to Huang’s return, too. The president — whose investment accounts traded up to $97 million worth of Nvidia stock since returning to office — initially floated the idea of having former Apple CEO Tim Cook take Huang’s place, before saying that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” to bring Huang back. This past weekend, Trump appears to have inserted himself into the situation directly. A report from The New York Times says that Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and Nvidia’s board to “resolve the situation,” while the Trump administration reassured the board that it “did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk.” Semafor reports that Trump even called in to Nvidia’s board meeting to advocate for Huang’s reinstatement. Sunday evening, Trump said in a post on Truth Social that he hopes Nvidia’s board “rehires Jensen Huang.” Hours later, Nvidia’s board did just that. The board announced on Monday that it reinstated Huang as its CEO, president, and board member. In its statement, the board said that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Trump immediately took credit for Huang’s reinstatement, with White House spokesperson Steven Cheung saying the president “was totally involved” in the decision. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said during an interview with CNBC. He added in a post on Truth Social that the US attorney general confirmed that it doesn’t have evidence that Huang “engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Nvidia’s shares rose on the news of Huang’s reinstatement, while tech leaders celebrated his return on social media. But the saga is likely far from over. The board said it will finish its investigation into Huang, the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Nvidia’s “accounting practices,” and Megaspeed is being investigated by the Justice Department. Even Trump has said that Nvidia should continue its internal investigation about export controls compliance. Trump’s apparent involvement also leaves plenty of room for scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who will control the House and Senate next year. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) called Nvidia’s decision “reckless” and urged the Trump administration to explain the “input” government officials provided to the company’s board. Huang’s stunning reinstatement still leaves many questions unanswered. Even though the backing of Wall Street, the White House, and Silicon Valley may have brought Huang back as CEO, a new wave of scrutiny from federal regulators and lawmakers is just getting started.

articles.title: Huang gets raucous ovation in return to Nvidia headquarters

I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees in a video Ming-Yu Liu, the…
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, back in charge after the company’s board of directors reinstated him Monday, returned to the tech giant’s headquarters to a loud ovation.

“Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees in a video Ming-Yu Liu, the company’s vice president of research, shared to the social platform X.

Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., after the board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Earlier this month, Jensen Huang resigned from the chipmaking company he founded amid reports about his extramarital affairs — including two with Nvidia employees and one with an alleged Chinese spy.

But in announcing Jensen Huang’s return , Nvidia’s board of directors said they were “satisfied” regarding his “candor” on the matter. The board also said Jensen Huang’s reinstatement “poses no national security risk,” citing input from “senior levels” of the U.S. government.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s board chair, said in a statement.

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company,” he added.

Jensen Huang said in the company’s release he was “honored” to return to Nvidia and “lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world.” The Nvidia CEO remains the subject of an independent investigation into his alleged affair with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy.

President Trump said Monday he “convinced” the Nvidia board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Jensen Huang, an ally of the president, successfully lobbied the administration last year to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 chips to China .

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday . “And I convinced them. I made the deal.”

Even after his return to Nvidia, Jensen Huang will still face scrutiny on Capitol Hill. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said Monday that Jensen Huang will testify before the panel on Dec. 3 .

articles.title: Billionaires spent $378 million to sink Prop 40. Norway’s 134-year-old wealth tax offers a different model
articles.summary: Norway’s 1% levy reaches the middle class and raises modest sums. U.S. plans target 938 billionaires at 5%, inviting flight and a court fight.
articles.body:
When Norway instituted a wealth tax in 1892, the U.S. was in the throes of the Gilded Age. American industrialists like John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie rocketed to unprecedented levels of wealth, while staggering economic inequality plagued the country.

More than 130 years later, Norway still levies that tax. And once again, the U.S. is experiencing an extraordinary degree of wealth concentration—by some measures, even exceeding Gilded Age levels.

The parallel now sits at the center of a live American debate. On Nov. 3, California voters rejected a one-time tax on billionaires even as they and voters in two other states backed higher income taxes on the rich . In Congress, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna are pushing an annual 5% federal tax on billionaire fortunes. In Norway, a government-appointed commission recommended this year that the country cut its rate.

The two countries are working from very different blueprints. Norway's tax reaches the middle class at about 1%. The leading U.S. proposals would hit fewer than 1,000 people at 5%. That difference shapes how much a wealth tax would raise, who would leave, and whether it would survive in court.

Unlike the billionaire-centric levies that have dominated the U.S. debate, Norway's wealth tax reaches a much broader slice of the population. For 2026, net wealth above NOK 1.9 million (about $197,000) is taxed at a combined local and national rate of 1% , with the threshold doubled for married couples. Above NOK 21.5 million (about $2.2 million), the rate rises to 1.1%.

Its contribution to government revenue is humbler than some advocates might expect. The tax generated about 0.6% of GDP and 1.5% of the country's total tax revenue in 2024, according to Cristina Enache, an economist at the Tax Foundation. That modest yield is one reason economists caution against treating Norway as proof that a U.S. version would generate enormous sums.

The tax has proved durable nonetheless. Its revenue has climbed despite an exodus of millionaires, Reuters reported last year . In a poll taken before Norway's September 2025 election, 39% of Norwegians wanted the tax kept or raised, 23% wanted it cut, and 28% wanted it abolished.

Norway, though, is rethinking the dose. In June, a government-appointed expert commission proposed cutting the rate to a single level between 0.25% and 0.75%.

Even in Norway, a wealth tax is not the main reason the country has built such a large public balance sheet. Its sovereign wealth fund, the largest in the world, is funded primarily by petroleum revenues, including taxes, licensing fees, and state ownership interests, not wealth-tax receipts. Norway's broader prosperity also reflects strong institutions, natural-resource wealth, high labor-force participation, and good governance, which makes it a hard template for the U.S. to replicate.
