articles.title: GOP senators urge Trump to support congressional ban on intoxicating hemp
articles.summary: More than a dozen Senate Republicans called on President Trump not to support any legislation that would delay the upcoming Dec. 11 deadline that will effectively ban intoxicating hemp products. In a letter sent Friday, Sens. Ted Budd (R-N.C.), Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) and 12 other Republicans said Trump should let Congress close the so-called hemp loophole “once…
articles.body:
More than a dozen Senate Republicans called on President Trump not to support any legislation that would delay the upcoming Dec. 11 deadline that will effectively ban intoxicating hemp products.

In a letter sent Friday, Sens. Ted Budd (R-N.C.), Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) and 12 other Republicans said Trump should let Congress close the so-called hemp loophole “once and for all.”

“The choice is simple: stand with American families who don’t want candy-flavored drugs sold in gas stations or with the cartel who profits from addiction and devastation,” the senators wrote. “There can be no last-minute ‘framework’ that keeps these drugs on store shelves.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Trump last year signed a ban on intoxicating hemp into law as part of a broader spending bill to reopen the government after a record-long shutdown.

The provision was set to take effect Nov. 11, but the hemp industry got a one-month reprieve when the Trump administration inserted a delay on the effective date into the government funding bill that passed in August— reportedly at the behest of Susie Wiles, the former White House chief of staff who was replaced earlier this month.

An amendment from Budd and Ricketts failed to gain support, and leadership was able to pass the final bill without it.

The delay expires Dec. 11, and without additional action the original ban would take effect on that date.

“Your Administration made clear at the time that there would be no further extensions. We ask that you hold to that commitment,” the senators wrote.

The lawmakers said Trump should not support any federal framework that would regulate intoxicating hemp instead of banning it.

A bill introduced last week by Sens. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) seeks to do just that.

Among other provisions, it would bar sales of consumable hemp products to people younger than 21 years, raise the legal threshold for THC-containing hemp, and ban “gas station” marijuana products derived from hemp.

The senators said a framework “is a permanent legal license for an industry that has spent years marketing drugs to kids, and it would create an additional federal sanctioned THC market that operates with no rules and no ability for states to regulate on their own.”

The issue in question concerns a law passed late last year that redefined hemp to close what critics called the “hemp loophole.”

The 2018 farm bill removed hemp from the controlled substances list.

But the law’s broad definition and subsequent lack of federal regulation created a loophole that allowed companies to extract and synthesize high levels of THC, the psychoactive compound in marijuana responsible for a high.

Those cannabinoid products, including gummies and drinks, have exploded in popularity and are now sold beyond dispensaries, expanding to gas stations, convenience stores and even major retailers such as Target.

Many can give people a marijuana-like high without being considered marijuana. They are sold without consistent age restrictions or labeling regulations and often resemble candy.

The new definition limits legal hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container of total THC, or any other cannabinoids with similar effects, far less than what most popular products contain.

articles.title: Water supply hack warning: FBI says threats are rising
articles.summary: Experts warn the next major target could be something essential to all: the water coming from your tap.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Recent tech outages have disrupted airlines, retailers and hospitals, but experts warn the next major target could be something far more essential: the water coming from your tap.

Federal agencies, researchers and cybersecurity experts are sounding alarms about rising threats to U.S. water systems as hackers increasingly target vulnerable infrastructure connected to the Internet.

The FBI warned in July that malicious cyber actors have been targeting Internet-facing programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, used by water and wastewater systems.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

According to the FBI, these intrusions have already caused operational disruptions, highlighting how vulnerable critical infrastructure can be when equipment is exposed online.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) warned in September that cyberattacks against public water systems are increasing.

The agency says utilities face threats ranging from ransomware to sophisticated intrusions that could disrupt operations or affect service reliability.

A recent report from The Pew Charitable Trusts found that many drinking water and wastewater systems operate with aging technology, limited budgets and staffing shortages that can hinder cybersecurity efforts.

Pew reported that local governments are increasingly investing in cyber defenses, but many smaller systems still struggle to keep pace with evolving threats.

Researchers Susan Athey, Neil Gandal, and Tyler Moore at Stanford Graduate School of Business say in their report “A Wake-Up Call on Cyber Risk as AI Ups the Stakes” that artificial intelligence is accelerating the cyber threat environment by helping attackers identify vulnerabilities more quickly and execute attacks at greater scale.

“The most severe cyber incidents can lead to losses amounting to billions of dollars and also have the potential to result in physical harm, loss of life, or even political turmoil,” they state in the report.

According to a recent Time analysis , cyberattacks have already affected water facilities in several states, including an incident in Minnesota that disrupted equipment at a treatment plant and threatened the local water supply.

Many small water systems remain vulnerable because they lack dedicated cybersecurity resources, making resilience and emergency preparedness increasingly important as threats grow.

Federal guidance urges utilities to strengthen cyber hygiene by disconnecting unnecessary Internet-facing devices, implementing multifactor authentication, conducting regular vulnerability assessments and maintaining incident response plans.

The FBI and EPA have encouraged operators to monitor industrial control systems closely and promptly apply security updates when available.

Experts say households should prepare for potential service disruptions much like they would for severe weather or power outages.

That can include maintaining an emergency supply of bottled water, storing water safely for sanitation needs, keeping basic emergency kits and monitoring instructions from local authorities if a utility reports an incident.

NewsNation’s Jesse Weber recently spoke with preparedness expert Jim Cobb, who said, “My longstanding recommendation has always been have enough cash immediately accessible” for fuel, lodging and meals during an emergency.

Cobb also advised households to review supplies already on hand before rushing to stores, adding that food, water and basic necessities should be a priority.

Why does this matter beyond cybersecurity?

Water systems are among the most critical pieces of infrastructure in the country, serving millions of Americans every day.

While major cyberattacks remain relatively rare, federal officials, researchers and industry experts agree that growing digital threats, combined with increasingly connected systems, mean cybersecurity is no longer just an IT problem.

articles.title: Trump Barges Into Nvidia's Internal Decisions, Opens Door to Even More Federal Meddling in the Economy
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s reinstatement means Washington will be intervening even more in the chip business.
articles.body:
On Monday, Nvidia's board of directors announced that it had "voted unanimously" to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The decision—which happened 11 days after Huang resigned following allegations that he had an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy—has shown just how entangled the federal government has become in the private sector, especially during the second Trump administration .

The decision to reinstate Huang has surprised some in Washington, D.C., and on Wall Street. On an earnings call with investors last Tuesday, Harvey Jones, Nvidia's board chair, said the board did not "intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." On Monday, the board reversed course. It said its decision followed a "series of discussions and meetings" with Huang, during which it felt "satisfied" with his "candor and ability to lead" Nvidia. In reaching its decision, Nvidia's board said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and was "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk." Semafor reported that hours before Nvidia's board made its final decision, President Donald Trump "dialed into Nvidia's board meeting to argue for Jensen Huang's return." The outlet also reported that Vice President J.D. Vance was "personally engaged" in Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang, because Vance and Trump believe that Huang is an "effective counterbalance against the incredible and increasing power of OpenAI and Anthropic."

The stock market has rallied in response to Huang's return. So too have lawmakers, who are calling for more intervention in the AI industry.

Following Nvidia's announcement, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D–Mass.) wrote that Congress should pass "bipartisan export control bills and make sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk." In the House, Rep. Don Bacon (R–Neb.) said Nvidia should have "moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang." Bacon also called for an investigation into "who approved high end computer chips sales to China." Warren and Bacon aren't alone in thinking export controls are necessary to maintain America's position in the AI race. In August 2025, and again in December of the same year, the Trump administration tried to curb sales to China by instituting export controls on Nvidia's advanced semiconductor chips, which it later eased.

Despite bipartisan calls from lawmakers to strictly regulate Nvidia—and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent telling Fox News that Nvidia needed a "dramatic shake-up" and alleging it had a "culture of non-compliance"—Trump remains a staunch supporter and advocate of Huang. In a Truth Social post sent after the decision was announced, Trump said that the "United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security." The president also said that Attorney General Todd Blanche had "confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence" that Huang "engaged in any unlawful conduct."

articles.title: Polymarket, Kalshi didn’t outperform mainstream forecasts in midterms: Report
articles.summary: A small group of sophisticated traders collected the vast majority of profits from bets on this month’s congressional midterm elections on Polymarket, while thousands of ordinary bettors lost money, according to a new report released Monday. The analysis by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, a nonprofit research group, found that just 819 accounts on Polymarket’s offshore…
articles.body:
A small group of sophisticated traders collected the vast majority of profits from bets on this month’s congressional midterm elections on Polymarket, while thousands of ordinary bettors lost money, according to a new report released Monday.

The analysis by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective , a nonprofit research group, found that just 819 accounts on Polymarket’s offshore platform made a combined $23.2 million in profits from congressional election bets. The top 82 accounts alone collected 55 percent of all profits, while the remaining 99 percent of accounts collectively lost $15 million.

The findings cast doubt on the broader benefits of the booming prediction market industry, which has touted its ability to accurately forecast election outcomes by allowing users to wager money on politics.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“Prediction markets create real risks to election integrity that cannot be ignored, while concentrating the financial rewards on a select few,” the report said.

Researchers found that prediction markets performed about as well as traditional election forecasting models in this year’s midterms, despite collecting millions of dollars in fees from traders.

“There is little learned exclusivity from prediction markets not already captured by one of the high-quality available forecast models,” the report said.

Kalshi, Polymarket and Polymarket US collectively generated an estimated $11.7 million in fees from election trading, with Kalshi accounting for the largest share, according to the report.

The study examined more than $180 million in wagers across nearly 6,000 congressional election markets on Polymarket, where roughly 82,000 accounts participated.

More than half of those accounts lost money, according to the report. Researchers also found that 42 percent of accounts lost money on every congressional race they wagered on.

The biggest winners were disproportionately professional traders and automated accounts. Researchers identified 6,824 accounts as either high-volume traders or bots, which represented just 8 percent of all accounts but accounted for 45 percent of betting activity and 72 percent of profits.

One account alone made $3.1 million betting on which party would control the House and Senate.

The findings come weeks after prediction market platforms celebrated their performances in the midterms, when Democrats swept into power in Congress and traders correctly anticipated many of the election’s most shocking outcomes.

articles.title: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine: Analysis
articles.summary: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in Moscow’s war in Ukraine, according to an analysis released Monday. The staggering figure — more people than the U.S. has lost in every war it has fought over the past 150 years combined — was found using new data from the Russian state statistics service gained…
articles.body:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in Moscow’s war in Ukraine, according to an analysis released Monday.

The staggering figure — more people than the U.S. has lost in every war it has fought over the past 150 years combined — was found using new data from the Russian state statistics service gained by pro-Ukraine hackers. The data was calculated by exiled Russian publications Meduza and Mediazona after it was released to media outlets. It did not address how many soldiers have been wounded.

The number of dead Kremlin soldiers highlights the sheer amount of human capital Russian President Vladimir Putin is willing to expend in his war to gain control of Ukraine, a conflict he began more than four years ago that has become Europe’s deadliest since World War II.

The figure also is a sharp uptick from the number of nearly 500,000 dead Russian troops revealed by the United Kingdom’s spy chief in late May.

Putin has not released accurate information on the war’s casualties to the Russian public and represses facts that would allow citizens to understand the scale and cost of the conflict.

Moscow initially sought to decapitate the Ukrainian government in a matter of days when it sent more than 150,000 troops into the country in February 2022, but the Russians were quickly mired by fierce Ukrainian opposition and issues with supplies.

The Russian troops were slowed or stopped by Ukrainian units using hit-and-run tactics and Western-supplied weapons, and Moscow within a month had lost an estimated 15,000 soldiers and had food, fuel and cold weather gear shortages.

The war has since shifted into a battle of attrition, with Ukraine making incremental gains thanks to its quick mastery of drone warfare that has allowed it to strike further and further across Russian borders, destroying Kremlin oil and military facilities and stopping Moscow’s battlefield gains.

Just this week, Ukrainian drones sank a Russian naval ship in a Libyan port, according to President Volodymyr ‌Zelensky.

There also is little public information on Ukrainian losses, though the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in July estimated that some 150,000 Ukrainian troops had been killed in the war through June.

articles.title: Fed's Williams: Fed must be forward-looking to bring inflation down
articles.summary: Williams noted that it's the Fed's job to make sure that higher energy prices, tariffs, and price increases from AI do not lead to broader or persistent infl...
articles.body:
New York Federal Reserve president John Williams said Monday that the central bank needs to be "forward-looking" on inflation and that there's still work to do to bring down prices.

"Monetary policy works with a lag of one to two years for its maximal effect on the economy," Williams said in a speech in New York. "Therefore, it is essential that we remain forward-looking and not overly focused on inflation's path in the past."

Williams noted that it's the Fed's job to make sure that higher energy prices, tariffs, and price increases from AI do not lead to broader or persistent inflation, saying that the Fed "must take actions over time" that ensure inflation gets back to the central bank's 2% goal in a timely manner.

"There is still work to do to get that done," he said.

Williams said he expects that data since the Fed's October policy meeting will show inflation has continued to run too high.

That Williams said the Fed needs to be more forward-looking does not match the approach the Fed has taken in recent years. The central bank has tended to be data-dependent, which is inherently more backward-looking. Williams didn't suggest that the Fed not consult data, but rather that any actions taken today will take a year or two to be implemented. With energy prices coming down, a lot could change.

Williams previously threw cold water on the prospect of a jumbo rate hike . When asked whether that latest inflation data calls for a supersize rate hike soon, Williams said, "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action."

Williams estimates a rate of 3.5% this year, but he sees it slowing to just above 2% next year as the effects of tariffs move further away, energy prices normalize, and the demand and supply of AI-related goods move back toward better balance.

While much of the overall strength in the economy can be traced to the AI-related boom and consumer spending, Williams said he sees a "two-track" economy where important parts are strong, but growth is at or below its trend rate.

He noted that sectors like residential investment and non-AI-related structures investment have weakened further over the past several quarters. This weakness also showed up in recent surveys the New York Fed conducted with businesses in the New York area, which report that while manufacturing is strong, business activity in the services sector has fallen sharply.

"This leaves us at an unusual macroeconomic juncture," Williams said. "The economic data are strong. The labor market is stable. And this strength is not creating macroeconomic imbalances in the labor market. Despite this overall balance, high inflation is proving persistent."

Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram .

articles.title: Why Nvidia’s board changed its mind on Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO on Monday, leaving Washington and Wall Street with myriad questions about how the company’s board of directors changed its mind in a matter of days. The board faced pressure on multiple fronts — from the Trump administration, Silicon Valley leaders and slumping markets — amid concerns about Nvidia’s future…
articles.body:
Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO on Monday, leaving Washington and Wall Street with myriad questions about how the company’s board of directors changed its mind in a matter of days.

The board faced pressure on multiple fronts — from the Trump administration , Silicon Valley leaders and slumping markets — amid concerns about Nvidia’s future without Jensen Huang at the helm.

President Trump quickly took credit for his role in Nvidia’s change of heart, which the board attributed to conversations with the company’s longtime CEO and input from “senior levels” of the U.S. government.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement marks a drastic turn of events, less than two weeks after he resigned from the tech giant due to a scandal over an alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

At the heart of the various forces working in Jensen Huang’s favor were the broader concerns about the company’s central role in the artificial intelligence boom and whether it could continue to thrive without his leadership.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly,” Trump told CNBC on Monday morning. “I felt very strongly about it. And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was to me, a very important part of our country.”

Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO and president, just days after telling investors it was not considering his return. He stepped down from the company earlier this month amid a series of affair scandals.

The move sent markets reeling. Nvidia’s chips are crucial to the AI boom, powering the technology’s development. Now one of the most valuable companies in the world, the chipmaker is a major driver of the stock market.

Jensen Huang immediately found support from a powerful contingent of Silicon Valley leaders.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk; Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick; Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney; and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan joined more than 170,000 others in signing an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s return last week.

David Sacks, former White House AI and cryptocurrency czar, also called into question the “spy narrative” surrounding Chinese business executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of passing information to Beijing while allegedly having an affair with the Nvidia CEO.

Jensen Huang noted last week that he received an “outpouring of calls” from Nvidia staff, investors, business partners and customers for his return, adding he would be “honored” to come back. But the board signaled it was unwilling to play ball.

The Trump administration appears to have put its thumb on the scale in Jensen Huang’s favor.

“I spoke to them, let me just put it that way, and I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago.”

Vice President Vance was also personally involved with the push to reinstate Jensen Huang, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill, underscoring his long-standing ties to Silicon Valley.

Wall Street was quick to celebrate Jensen Huang’s return, following uncertainty about whether Nvidia could maintain its dominance without the longtime CEO.

“I do not believe there is another executive who could effectively replicate his vision, leadership, or understanding of where artificial intelligence is heading,” Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, said in a statement.

Nvidia’s stock climbed more than 30 percent Monday, and the Nasdaq composite and S&P 500 shot up as well.

This followed more than a week of market whiplash for Nvidia, which hit a 52-week closing low of $125.53 last Friday. But analysts warned Jensen Huang’s departure was bigger than Nvidia and threatened the overall stability of the AI industry and market as a whole.

“This underscores that enough people believe that our economy and national security are not just dependent on one company, but on one man,” Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser at the White House’s National Economic Council and Office of Science & Tech Policy, said in a statement Monday.

When asked by CNBC whether the significant tech sell-off in the markets last week influenced his reasoning, Trump said, “Probably so, but the biggest impact was long term.”

The president said he isn’t concerned anymore “because we have one of our great stars back in play.”

Tech analyst Dan Ives suggested the board reversed its stance “because the alternative, a founder-less Nvidia at the start of the Rubin cycle with a CEO search running into next year, was the bigger risk to shareholders.”

“At the end of the day despite this Jensen saga the Board knew it had no choice but to bring him back and for the US technology sector this was the move it had to make,” Ives wrote in a note for Yorkville Ives & Co. on Monday.

Still, Ives said he is not changing his price target on Nvidia, given the numerous factors still in play, including the independent committee’s investigation into Jensen Huang’s actions.

But not all are happy on Wall Street, warning of the implications of the move.

“When the CEO of the world’s most valuable company is infiltrated by a Chinese spy and we ignore that because the share price went down? That’s a society that is focused on its own immediate gratification ahead of logic or long-term thinking,” Bradley Tusk, founder and CEO of Tusk Ventures, said to The Hill.

“It’s just short-term optics,” Peter Ricchiuti, professor of finance at Tulane University’s Freeman School of Business, told The Hill. “If you’re a shareholder on a short-term basis, you’re very excited but it doesn’t say much.”

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement sparked an outcry from lawmakers of both parties , who vowed to continue their investigations into Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who reportedly took a softer tone on the company over its stance on exporting some AI chips to China.

The Nvidia CEO is scheduled to appear for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 in front of three House committees — the Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence Committee and the Select Committee on China. Jensen Huang will then testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. Lutnick has also agreed to appear before Congress on the matter.

articles.title: Clayton to serve as interim national cyber director
articles.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has been tapped to serve as interim national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation, according to a White House official. Davies, who has served as the Pentagon’s chief information officer since last year, was named the acting director of the White House’s Office of the National Cyber…
articles.body:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has been tapped to serve as interim national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation, according to a White House official.

Davies, who has served as the Pentagon’s chief information officer since last year, was named the acting director of the White House’s Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD) following the departure of Sean Cairncross .

Clayton said in a statement he is looking forward to “working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into her role.”

A White House official said President Trump decided to nominate Davies to be the national cyber director following the support she received from industry and government officials last week when he named her the acting director of the office.

While awaiting her confirmation, Davies will be a senior advisor for the agency to assist Clayton, the official added.

The official pointed to Clayton’s involvement with cybersecurity policy, including through his role as chair of the White House’s Super Intelligence Force . He was also named Trump’s AI — or “SI,” as the president calls it — czar to oversee the government’s policy on the technology’s development.

“I’m excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director,” Clayton said.

Cairncross was let go as national cyber director last week and a White House official later said the president believed he did not have the proper cyber credentials for the job.

While the Office of the National Cyber Director has often managed to keep a lower profile in past presidencies, the advancements of AI have propelled cybersecurity concerns to the forefront over the past year as the tool becomes a potential weapon for adversaries and hackers.

The agency manages cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government.

Cairncross reportedly clashed with other leaders of the president’s Cabinet on these issues.

He allegedly believed the Treasury Department had become too involved with the team’s efforts, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his allies argued Cairncross had not been urgent with responding to questions about AI, according to Axios, which first reported on his departure.

articles.title: First new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer approved in decades
articles.summary: The new treatment is for early stage, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The Food and Drug Administration approved a new treatment for early-stage, estrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, the first new hormone therapy for early-stage cancer in more than 20 years.

The FDA approved giredestrant, under the brand name Wilserdly, as a post-surgery treatment for adults with the most common subtype of breast cancer for patients with Stage 1, 2 or 3 disease.

Breast cancer is the second most common cancer among women in the U.S., and roughly 70% of breast cancers are hormone receptor-positive, which means estrogen fuels the growth of the cancer.

Traditionally, people with early-stage, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer are treated with surgery followed by endocrine therapy , including drugs like tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor. However, some patients struggle with the side effects of those drugs, and recurrence is still a concern.

Wilserdly has been approved for use alone after surgery and comes as a once-daily oral tablet. It belongs to a class of drugs known as oral estrogen receptor antagonists, which help block estrogen from binding to receptors on cancer cells and break down the receptors, helping to block tumor growth.

“For patients with early-stage hormone-driven breast cancer, the goal after surgery is to keep the cancer from coming back,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence. “Our review focused on whether Wilserdly could reduce that risk more effectively than the hormone therapies patients already receive. The evidence showed that it could, supporting today’s approval of a new option for patients at intermediate to high risk of recurrence.”

In a randomized trial, Wilserdly reduced the risk of invasive breast cancer recurrence or death by 30% compared to standard hormone therapy. After three years, 92.4% of patients taking Wilserdly were alive and had no invasive breast cancer, compared to 89.6% of those receiving traditional hormone therapy.

Side effects of Wilserdly include muscle and joint pain, hot flashes, tiredness, headache, nausea, slower heart rate, dizziness, numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, increased liver enzymes, lower blood counts, high blood fat levels and changes in kidney test results.

Wilserdly can harm a developing fetus if taken during pregnancy, and women who have not completed menopause need additional hormone-suppressing medication. Men with breast cancer can also take Wilserdly.

articles.title: Medications recalled nationwide, including some GLP-1 injections
articles.summary: “Use of a drug product intended to be sterile, that is not sterile, could result in serious infections,” the pharmacy warned.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A Texas compounding pharmacy is voluntarily recalling specific lots of medication over sterility concerns.

Greenwich Rx said in a release that the recall applies to various compounded sterile products dispensed nationwide between Aug. 10 and Sept. 21, 2026.

The recall was initiated after an FDA inspection and the pharmacy’s evaluation of the products raised concerns about a potential lack of sterility assurance, the release said. Semaglutide injections, a type of GLP-1 medication , were among the recalled medications.

Greenwich Rx is now notifying affected customers by mail, the release added. So far, the pharmacy hasn’t received any reports of adverse events related to the recall. Some of the products, however, were also compounded by Greenwich Rx for another pharmacy, Clover Rx.

“Customers who received medications through Clove Rx should review the affected product list, even if they have not received a direct recall notification,” the release noted. “Use of a drug product intended to be sterile, that is not sterile, could result in serious infections, which may be life threatening.”

The recall notice doesn’t specify brand names, so consumers should check the full list of affected products, including lot numbers and expiration dates, on the pharmacy’s website here to see whether their medications are impacted by the recall.

Consumers and clinics with the recalled medications should stop using them immediately and discard them. For questions, consumers can contact the company at 888-243-5547 or GreenwichRx6588@sedgwick.com during standard business hours.

articles.title: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
articles.summary: Ladybird is the first new web browser in years that isn’t built on Chrome or Firefox.
articles.body: Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling announced that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development. The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We’ve seen many engines emerge over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. While Gecko, now used in Mozilla Firefox, first appeared in Netscape 6 in 2000, Apple’s WebKit arrived in Safari in 2003 as a fork of KDE’s KHTML. A decade later, the Google-backed Chromium project forked WebKit to create Blink, which now powers Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera, and more. Ladybird is backed by a nonprofit organization with the goal of creating “an independent, fast and secure browser that respects user privacy and fosters an open web,” according to its website. Though Ladybird development initially began as part of a C++ project, its developers eventually began porting the code to Rust using AI. In his post announcing the alpha, Kling notes that the browser built around the Ladybird engine “is modest but functional,” adding that “some websites won’t work” during the alpha. A Windows version of Ladybird will arrive during a “later stage” of the project.

articles.title: Key House Democrat will oppose permitting reform bill
articles.summary: Rep. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) on Monday said he will oppose a Senate-passed bill that seeks to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy and infrastructure. Levin, a clean energy advocate, said in a statement that with the 2026 Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), “there’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment.”…
articles.body:
Rep. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) on Monday said he will oppose a Senate-passed bill that seeks to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy and infrastructure.

Levin, a clean energy advocate, said in a statement that with the 2026 Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), “there’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment.”

“The bill would modernize a power grid that too often can’t carry affordable clean energy to the homes that need it, and it would require data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades instead of passing the cost on to families,” he said.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

But he added that the bill raised concerns, including placing a limit on “California’s ability to protect its own water, weaken the science behind endangered species decisions, and keep courts from halting a project even when an agency skips the review the law requires.”

Levin also pointed to President Trump’s approvals for offshore leases and said BAAJA would make it “extremely hard” for future presidential administrations to overturn the law.

“For those of us who have spent years fighting to keep new oil rigs off the California coast, that’s a serious threat,” he said.

“Tribal nations have warned that the bill’s changes to historic preservation law could endanger sacred sites and undercut Tribal sovereignty, and they deserved a far bigger voice in writing it,” Levin continued. “Those harms would be permanent, while the clean energy gains would rise or fall with whoever happens to be carrying out the law.”

He said that the latest iteration of the bill would be “giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.”

“There’s still time to get this right. If House and Senate leaders from both parties sit down together and negotiate sufficient changes, I’ll be ready to vote yes,” he said.

Levin represents California’s 49th Congressional District, which straddles between northern San Diego County and southern Orange County, encompassing the cities of Carlsbad, Dana Point, San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.

Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) echoed Levin’s concerns in his own statement, saying the two congressmen have worked “extensively on this issue.” He said the country “does not struggle to build data centers or gas pipelines.”

“Instead, we consistently struggle to build cheaper, cleaner energy sources that would successfully compete against existing fossil fuel assets but are blocked by the incumbent interests,” he said, adding that BAAJA’s “problems … can be fixed.”

“Climate change and permitting reform are too important to settle for anything less than a deal that unleashes our economy and protects our communities,” he added.

The Senate passed BAAJA 62-33 last Thursday, spearheaded by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) Sens. Mike Rounds (S.D.) and Josh Hawley (Mo.) were the only Republicans to vote against the bill, while 15 Democrats voted in favor of the bill.

Other opponents of the bill say it would bolster fossil fuels and mining, loosen environmental laws and limit the ability of a project’s opponents to challenge it in court.

Supporters say it will build the U.S. economy and allow for upgrades to the country’s infrastructure, including energy, to commence faster. They also say it will help lower the nation’s planet-warming emissions.

Yet the bill faces a crowded lame-duck calendar, including a possible lapse in federal funding, with some Democratic lawmakers deliberating over how to respond to funds going toward the Iran war or risk a government shutdown.

articles.title: Commerce Department adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist amid Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: The Commerce Department moved to add Megaspeed — the company at the center of Nvidia’s national security scandal — to its trade entity blacklist on Monday, according to federal records. The move, published in the Federal Register on Monday, comes as scrutiny mounts on the Commerce Department to tighten its chip export controls following reports…
articles.body:
The Commerce Department moved to add Megaspeed — the company at the center of Nvidia’s national security scandal — to its trade entity blacklist on Monday, according to federal records.

The move, published in the Federal Register on Monday, comes as scrutiny mounts on the Commerce Department to tighten its chip export controls following reports Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle Nvidia’s chips to China.

The allegations surfaced amid reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with onetime Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspected of spying for China.

According to the Federal Register, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) made the decision for Megaspeed and six entities after determining “significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.”

Semafor first reported the BIS designation Monday.

As details around Jensen Huang’s alleged affair unfolded earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the Trump administration’s failure to place Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, on the U.S. trade blacklist for national security concerns.

“Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent told CNBC this month. “But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly took a softer line on Nvidia over the tech giant’s AI chip sales to China and Axios reported Bessent confronted the Commerce chief earlier this month about the delay. Lutnick, according to Axios, told Bessent he would “look into it.”

The allegations of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang prompted his resignation as Nvidia’s CEO and president less than two weeks ago, but the company’s board of directors took a sharp reversal and unanimously voted to reinstate him Monday.

The Nvidia CEO is scheduled to appear for a closed-door briefing on Dec. 1 in front of three House committees — the Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence Committee and the Select Committee on China. Jensen Huang will then testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

Lutnick has also agreed to appear before Congress on the matter.

articles.title: Trump, Iowa’s Sand play hot potato with lead detonation call
articles.summary: Neither President Trump nor Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) appears to want ownership of a political hot potato as the Army considers detonating lead-containing munitions, stirring public outcry. While the Army had been poised to move ahead with the controversial Iowa detonation on Wednesday, Trump on Monday said he would not move forward with the…
articles.body:
Neither President Trump nor Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) appears to want ownership of a political hot potato as the Army considers detonating lead-containing munitions, stirring public outcry.

While the Army had been poised to move ahead with the controversial Iowa detonation on Wednesday, Trump on Monday said he would not move forward with the controlled demolition if Sand or the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals objected.

Neither did, and Sand released a statement saying, “The Administration should make this decision.”

Regardless of who ultimately makes the call, Iowans in the immediate area could be at risk of exposure to lead, which is neurotoxic to children.

“It seems like coming to the conclusion of a controlled explosion is the best of a bad set of options,” said Alex Souchen, a professor at the University of Guelph in Canada who studies military history and pollution.

“It seems like they’re going to try to limit the release of any sort of toxic byproduct, but it’s going to cause a debris cloud regardless of what happens,” Souchen added.

Questions are being raised about how the situation got to this point in the first place.

“When the military says it’s discovering that there was an issue … what was happening before? How are they monitoring it? How did it just suddenly become an issue right now and not five months ago?” Souchen asked.

“That to me is the bigger question … the fact that there’s been a long-term storage problem, and what does that mean for the other ordnance that’s being stored at that facility? It kind of precipitates a whole series of questions about what types of protocols are in place, and the military seems to be portraying it as, ‘Well, we just discovered this issue,’ but clearly that issue has been ongoing for many years,” he added.

On Nov. 15, the Army issued a public advisory stating that in five days, it planned to detonate degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, resulting in a plume with lead-containing particles in the air.

Lead is a toxic metal that can be particularly harmful to babies and children. Exposure to lead in children can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, learning problems, behavioral issues and a lower IQ. In rare cases, it can also cause seizures, coma and death, according to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

In adults, lead exposure can cause decreased kidney function, heart-related issues and fertility issues.

“Lead doesn’t break down into something else; it just is lead. And so, if that dust gets transported through the air, wherever it lands … it will be there for some time, so … that means it’s going to be a longer-term exposure,” said Peter DeCarlo, a professor who studies air pollution at Johns Hopkins University.

“One of the things we worry about sometimes is if this dust can get into a home and it’s no longer airborne, but it’s on the ground … then it’s particularly potentially problematic for little kids who play on the floor and who are more prone to putting their hands in their mouth,” DeCarlo said.

An official environmental analysis of the detonation found that it “will result in the immediate, short-term generation of air pollutants” such as lead. But it added that not taking action would risk an “accidental, uncontrolled detonation” that could create “a large-scale hazardous debris field.”

The Army’s detonation plans and the short notice it provided stirred public outrage. Environmental organizations also sued over the EPA’s emergency permit for the activity. The detonation was eventually moved first to Monday and later to Wednesday.

Then, on Monday, Trump said that while he personally supported the detonation, he would leave the ultimate decision in the hands of the courts and Sand, who defeated Republican Zach Lahn for the state’s governorship earlier this month.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” the president added.

Sand kicked the can back to the White House, saying the federal government should make the call but adding that “Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward.”

Meanwhile, on Monday, the appeals court also declined to halt the detonation, denying an emergency request from environmental groups.

At press time Monday evening it was not immediately clear whether the detonation would proceed on Wednesday.

When the detonation was initially moved to Monday, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said that it needed to happen then because it was “prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

DeCarlo noted that regardless of whether an explosion is controlled or accidental, lead could still reach the air, but he said that if it is done “intentionally,” the government can have “a little bit more control over the situation.”

“If you want to pick a time in which the wind is blowing in a way that keeps it away from major cities, or that potentially it rains … that helps reduce the spread of that dust and keeps it more isolated to a particular location,” he said.

While public awareness of the situation is new, the federal government had significantly more notice.

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” said an unsigned joint statement from the Army, EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services.

The EPA provided the statement to The Hill but did not address specific questions. The Army did not respond to questions from The Hill.

The New York Times first reported that the Army had also been considering a separate option: chemically treating the munitions instead of detonating them. Such a plan would offer “environmental protections by avoiding a blast plume,” and would process the Iowa stockpile in 22 days or less, according to service documents.

But a company it had hired, MuniRem Environmental, said that the Army later canceled its contract.

“We’ve been told that it is for safety reasons. We haven’t had a detailed explanation for canceling the contract,” said MuniRem CEO Valentine Nzengung.

Nzengung added that he believes “chemical neutralization remains a viable option” for dealing with the Middletown munitions.

However, the government’s environmental analysis said that it eliminated chemical neutralization as an option because it requires “opening drums and physically agitating shock-sensitive crystals, creating an extreme and unacceptable risk of fatal accidental detonation.”

Despite the Army knowing about the unstable material for months, it has not released an evacuation plan or a map of the potential fallout, even as it has admitted a plume containing toxic lead could travel up to 20 miles away. The Iowa Environmental Council, however, places that estimate closer to 100 miles.

Questions remain as to how nearby farms and livestock, as well as vulnerable individuals who cannot relocate, will be affected by a detonation.

Souchen, from the University of Guelph, noted that military personnel could be among the most impacted.

“At the end of the day, whatever happens it’s going to be the people at the lower end of the command hierarchy that are going to be carrying out the orders and fulfilling the solution, and I think that they need to have a voice in this and be recognized because they’re in harm’s way,” he said.

articles.body:
Pennsylvania health officials on Monday confirmed the state’s ninth measles-related death this year, less than a week after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health said an unvaccinated Centre County resident died after testing positive for the virus. The state has recorded 1,638 measles cases across 46 counties this year, with 49 new infections confirmed as of Monday.

The number of hospitalizations has risen from 315 to 330. Only five of the confirmed infections have been among vaccinated individuals, according to the state’s measles dashboard .

An eighth measles-related death was reported last week, where an unvaccinated resident of Clinton County initially tested positive for the virus before their death.

Pennsylvania has been hit hard by the resurgence of measles, accounting for more than a quarter of infections nationwide so far. The outbreak, which began in late April, has prompted state health officials to expand vaccination efforts in affected communities.

The department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics, with dozens more planned in the coming weeks and months.

The demand for the vaccine has climbed considerably. Healthcare providers across Pennsylvania administered nearly 62,000 doses in October, compared to the roughly 25,000 in a typical month.

The latest measles-related death comes after the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced last week that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status after 25 years, officially making the U.S. a country where measles is endemic.

The resurgence of measles amid the Trump administration’s efforts to fuel speculation about the safety and efficacy of vaccines has sparked tensions between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine skeptic.

Shapiro has accused Kennedy and other administration officials of spreading misinformation about vaccines and disrupting public trust in public health, which the HHS secretary has denied doing.

The Army’s plan to detonate tons of explosive lead material in Iowa is in limbo on Monday after Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) passed the decision back to President Trump and a federal appeals court declined to intervene.

The Army was poised to detonate the munitions last week but had postponed the action to this Wednesday amid public outcry .

It has said in official documents that handling the munitions in a controlled way would be better than leaving them alone because it would avoid the risk of an “accidental, uncontrolled detonation” that could lead to “catastrophic damage.”

But an official environmental analysis of the detonation found that it “will result in the immediate, short-term generation of air pollutants ” such as lead.

“The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks. articles.title: Army sergeant pleads guilty to cashing in on US military secrets in China-linked plot, DOJ says
articles.summary: Sgt. Jian Zhao faces up to 10 years in prison after pleading guilty to selling national defense information from Joint Base Lewis-McChord, prosecutors say.
articles.body: An active-duty U.S. Army sergeant pleaded guilty Monday in a yearslong plot that turned his access to sensitive military information into a payday from buyers in China. Jian Zhao, 37, used his personal cellphone to photograph restricted Army documents, handed over excerpts from technical manuals for the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, or HIMARS, and put military computers and government hard drives up for sale, federal prosecutors said. "Protecting our national security depends on holding accountable those who compromise their oath and endanger the security of our armed forces," U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford wrote on X. CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN "Jian Zhao violated that trust by exploiting his access to military information and equipment for personal profit while knowingly providing materials to individuals linked to China." Zhao pleaded guilty to conspiring to gather, transmit and transfer national defense information. Prosecutors said he enlisted in 2017 and served as a battery supply sergeant at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington, where his duties and security clearance gave him access to sensitive Army information and equipment. CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN The documents Zhao photographed covered Army operations, communications networks, military exercises and rocket and missile systems, prosecutors said. He also took military storage devices without permission and collected thousands of dollars for materials he described as sensitive, secret or top secret. SENIOR US ARMY SOLDIER ARRESTED IN UK ON SUSPICION OF SPYING FOR RUSSIA "This guilty plea reflects a deliberate betrayal of the oath every Soldier takes to defend our nation and safeguard our fellow service members," said Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, who leads Army Counterintelligence Command. Stinchon said the scheme put soldiers at risk and urged troops to report suspicious activity or outreach. CALIFORNIA REALTOR NABBED AT LAX IN ALLEGED CHINA SPY CASE TARGETING TAIWAN PRESIDENT’S RELATIVE Prosecutors traced the plot back to late 2021. Ruoyu Duan, a former Army soldier living in Hillsboro, Oregon, recruited Zhao and other active-duty troops to provide defense information and helped arrange payments from buyers in China, prosecutors said. Duan previously pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defense information. Federal agents arrested Zhao at his home in Lacey, Washington, on March 6, 2025, and recovered about $30,000 in cash, electronic devices and multiple Army hard drives. FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR ADMITS TO SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING BEIJING PROPAGANDA IN US Under his plea agreement, Zhao agreed to forfeit $17,500 in proceeds from the scheme and give up his claim to the seized cash. "By pleading guilty, Jian Zhao has admitted to betraying that trust and abusing the responsibilities that came with his position and security clearance," said Doug Olson, the FBI’s special agent in charge in Portland. "Those who choose to compromise sensitive military information for personal gain put our nation's interests at risk, and the FBI, alongside our law enforcement and military partners, remains committed to holding them accountable," he continued.
